name: Sweet Potato
variety: Species-level edible sweetpotato; no cultivar or ornamental foliage selection assigned
summary: A warm-season crop grown from vegetative slips for edible storage roots; it is botanically unrelated to potato (Solanum tuberosum). Edible-root cultivars are distinct from ornamental foliage selections; neither a named cultivar nor ornamental type is assigned here.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ipomoea batatas in Convolvulaceae and distinguishes it from true potato, Solanum tuberosum. This species-level entry does not specify a root-flesh color, named cultivar, or ornamental foliage selection.

cultivation.short: Warm-season crop; frost-sensitive and suited to outdoor beds or large containers
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes sweetpotato as frost-sensitive, suited to full sun or partial shade and well-drained soil; it needs a long warm, frost-free growing period. Illinois Extension adds regional late-season moisture guidance: avoid excess irrigation and abrupt heavy rain after dry conditions, which can split developing roots. These outdoor recommendations do not establish hydroponic fit.

growth.short: Spreading vine with cultivar-dependent foliage and root performance
growth.guidance: The crop commonly forms spreading vines that can root at nodes; Illinois Extension notes that bush forms also exist. NC State distinguishes edible-root cultivars from ornamental foliage selections. Because this is an unspecified edible species-level identity, no single mature spread or cultivar performance is assigned.

harvest.short: Dig carefully before frost; timing depends on region and crop
harvest.guidance: Illinois Extension describes taking some roots in late summer while leaving the plant growing, then harvesting the main crop near the first fall frost in its regional context. Dig carefully to reduce root injury and adjust timing to local frost and cultivar; no universal maturity date or curing guarantee is assigned.

problems.short: Avoid frost and late-season water swings that can damage roots
problems.guidance: Frost can injure this warm-season crop. Illinois Extension notes that excess water or heavy rain after a dry period late in the season can split roots; poor drainage may produce long, misshapen roots. These are regional crop-management signals, not cultivar-specific disease or resistance claims.

propagation.short: Usually established from vegetative slips, not botanical seed
propagation.guidance: NC State Extension describes propagation from slips or rooted cuttings. The represented home-garden crop is vegetatively propagated; this material does not receive a Seed Profile, and no seed-start instructions are implied.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected extension source describes soil/container and groundcover growing, not a recirculating hydroponic crop system.

evidence.note: Species-level source describes spreading/vining growth; no cultivar-specific habit is assigned.

spread.reason: No single mature spread is selected for this cultivar-unspecified identity.

name: Potato
variety: Species-level cultivated potato; no cultivar, market class, or subspecies assigned
summary: A widely grown crop cultivated from seed tubers rather than botanical seed in ordinary home gardens. Thousands of cultivars differ in tuber form and culinary use; none is selected for this species-level entry.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Solanum tuberosum in Solanaceae. Minnesota Extension distinguishes vegetative seed tubers from true botanical seed; the common name seed potato refers to planting stock, not a Seed Profile material.

cultivation.short: Outdoor crop grown in loose, well-drained soil or sufficiently large containers
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension recommends full sun and well-drained soil; its regional container guidance specifies a grow bag at least 2 ft deep and 30 gal. UMN Extension describes hilling around shoots as they grow (the NC State guide places this around 1 ft tall) to keep developing tubers covered. These are outdoor soil/container practices, not a hydroponic prescription.

growth.short: Erect foliage produces underground stolons and tubers
growth.guidance: Kew and extension sources describe tuber-bearing underground shoots. Hilling is used in soil production to cover tubers and prevent light exposure; it is not a universal container or hydroponic instruction.

harvest.short: Harvest new or mature tubers according to crop stage
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension describes harvesting small new potatoes before skins thicken, with roughly 7–8 weeks given as a regional example; mature tubers are harvested after foliage dies back and skins set. Cultivar and local season affect timing, so this is not a universal schedule.

problems.short: Keep developing tubers covered and do not eat green plant parts
problems.guidance: Keep tubers covered because light can green them; do not eat green potatoes or green plant parts because the cited sources identify solanine risk. UMN also describes hollow heart associated with uneven moisture/growth, scab as rough corky patches, and Colorado potato beetle as a recognizable foliage-feeding pest. These are crop-level signals, not cultivar resistance claims.

propagation.short: Plant certified seed tubers or pieces with eyes; this is vegetative stock, not botanical seed
propagation.guidance: UMN Extension recommends disease-free seed potatoes and explains that planting pieces are tubers, not true botanical seed. Grocery potatoes may carry disease or be treated to inhibit sprouting, so their suitability is not assumed. No Seed Profile applies to this represented propagation material.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Selected sources document soil and large-container culture, not a reliable recirculating home hydroponic method.

evidence.note: NC State describes erect stems; this is species-level habit, not cultivar-specific.

height.reason: The selected source provides a range but no cultivar is represented; dimensions are left unresolved rather than implying precision.

spread.reason: No cultivar-specific mature spread is assigned.

spacing.reason: Regional soil row spacing cannot be converted into a hydroponic pod-spacing recommendation.

light.reason: Outdoor full-sun guidance is not translated into an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Garlic
variety: Species-level garlic; hardneck and softneck crop groups not selected; elephant garlic excluded
summary: A bulb crop commonly planted from individual cloves. Hardneck and softneck groups are types within Allium sativum; elephant garlic is a different species and is not included in this identity.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Allium sativum in Amaryllidaceae. Utah State Extension distinguishes hardneck and softneck garlic types from elephant garlic, Allium ampeloprasum; neither garlic type is assigned as a named cultivar here.

cultivation.short: Cool-season bulb crop; regional fall planting and well-drained soil guidance
cultivation.guidance: Utah State Extension recommends fall planting in its Utah context and emphasizes fertile, well-drained soil and moisture during growth. Its field spacing and fertilizer rates are not reused as indoor hydroponic instructions.

growth.short: One planted clove produces a bulb; hardneck may form a flowering scape
growth.guidance: Utah State Extension reports one bulb per planted clove and describes differences between hardneck and softneck types. Scape removal is mentioned only as a crop-management option when a scape forms, not as a property of every type.

care.short: Cut a flowering stem if one forms; keep weeding shallow and mulch
care.guidance: Utah State University Extension says a flowering stem, if it forms, can be cut to redirect more energy toward the bulb; this is conditional guidance, not a claim that every garlic type forms one. The same Utah guide emphasizes weed control during the first two months and shallow cultivation to avoid root injury. Organic mulch can conserve water, reduce weeds and protect outdoor garlic through winter. These are Utah garden-soil practices, not indoor-container or hydroponic instructions.

harvest.short: Harvest when tops yellow, before they become fully dry
harvest.guidance: Utah State Extension recommends lifting bulbs as tops yellow but before they are fully dry, then curing in a shaded warm location. Exact calendar timing depends on planting season and local conditions.

problems.short: Excess moisture near maturity can impair curing and storage
problems.guidance: Utah State Extension warns that excess water as foliage matures can delay curing and cause storage problems, and identifies thrips, onion maggot, and neck rot. These are source-level risks, not claims of resistance or universal susceptibility for a named selection.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected source documents soil-grown bulb production, not a recirculating home hydroponic method.

growthHabits.reason: The source describes bulb and leaf growth but does not map this identity to the controlled growth-habit vocabulary.

name: Ginger
summary: A tropical rhizomatous perennial grown for aromatic edible rhizomes. University of Vermont Extension documents home container growing indoors or outdoors in warm weather; this does not establish recirculating hydroponic fit.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Zingiber officinale in Zingiberaceae and identifies the rhizome as the spice source. No named cultivar or commercial ginger type is selected.

cultivation.short: Warm, humid, well-drained conditions; protect from cold
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes partial shade and rich soil. University of Vermont Extension's home-container method uses a pot at least 12 inches wide, temperatures of at least 68°F and never below 50°F, and soil kept moist—not wet—after growth begins. It recommends a sunny window, supplemental grow light if needed, and gradual outdoor acclimation in warm weather. These regional/home-container directions do not establish a numeric indoor-light tier or hydroponic fit.

growth.short: Clumping leafy shoots arise from branched underground rhizomes
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes an upright, clumping and spreading plant with species-level dimensions. Flower spikes arise on a separate leafless stem; young clumps may take two years to flower, and container plants rarely bloom. These are species observations, not a cultivar-specific performance promise.

flowering.short: Flowering is uncommon in containers and may take years
flowering.guidance: NC State Extension reports cone-shaped flower spikes on a separate leafless stem, says new clumps may not flower for two years, and notes container plants rarely bloom. Lack of flowers in a young or container-grown plant is not by itself evidence of a cultivation failure.

harvest.short: Choose partial rhizome harvest or a full seasonal lift
harvest.guidance: For a continuing clump, NC State Extension says to take several rhizomes carefully and leave the rest growing; young rhizomes are juicier and milder, while mature ones become more fibrous and pungent. UVM Extension describes lifting a home container after foliage yellows and dries, around 8–10 months in its method, then reserving sound pieces for replanting. These are distinct approaches, not one universal date.

problems.short: Cold, wet conditions risk root rot; strong sun can stress foliage
problems.guidance: NC State Extension warns that cold and/or wet conditions can cause root rot and that full sun may produce brown leaf tips and poor growth in its regional guidance. Treat brown tips as a stress cue, not a diagnosis or cultivar-specific susceptibility.

name: Turmeric
summary: A tropical rhizomatous perennial grown for its aromatic yellow-orange culinary rhizome. Extension sources document warm-climate garden and home-container growing; NC State reports sterile flowers, so no Seed Profile is represented for this identity.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Curcuma longa in Zingiberaceae and lists Curcuma domestica as a synonym. NC State Extension describes the culinary rhizome and does not assign a named cultivar.

cultivation.short: Warm, humid growing conditions; protect from cold and allow rhizome room
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension recommends hot, humid conditions, morning sun with afternoon shade, and moist but well-drained soil in its outdoor guidance; expanding rhizomes can split a container. UVM Extension documents home-container growing indoors or outdoors in warm weather, at least 68°F and never below 50°F, near a sunny window or with supplemental grow light if needed, and in soil kept moist but not wet. Container growing does not establish recirculating hydroponic suitability or a numeric indoor-light requirement.

growth.short: Upright clump with broad leaves from branched rhizomes
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes large lance-shaped leaves (up to about 40 inches in its account), roughly 8–12 leaves per shoot, and species-level mature dimensions. These are regional species observations, not cultivar guarantees.

flowering.short: Yellow-white summer flowers are sterile; viable seed is not reported
flowering.guidance: NC State Extension describes yellow-white flower spikes and reports that flowers are sterile and do not produce viable seeds. Rhizome division is the documented propagation route; this evidence does not establish a seed-start protocol.

harvest.short: Harvest when foliage yellows, wilts and dries
harvest.guidance: NC State Extension describes fall harvest as foliage begins to wilt and dry in its regional garden context. UVM Extension describes home-container harvest after foliage yellows and dries, around 8–10 months in its method. Use the foliage cue rather than treating either calendar as universal.

problems.short: Watch for dry-soil mites, slugs, cold stress and staining
problems.guidance: NC State Extension notes slugs or snails may affect young leaves and older plants may develop spider mites when soil is too dry; it reports no serious pest or disease problems in its regional account, not universal resistance. Yellow rhizome dye can stain skin and clothing and may cause an allergic skin reaction.
